summary: Defines a mechanism for conveying load information in Diameter, even when a node is not overloaded. RFC 7068 required this, and the DOIC solution in RFC 7683 did not include it. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of waiting until it is swamped, a server tells others how busy it is, so they can send work to the less busy ones.

questions: difference between load and overload in diameter
what is the diameter load avp
subtitle: How Diameter nodes can tell their peers how busy they are, long before they are actually overloaded.

tldr.problem: Diameter overload control (DOIC, RFC 7683) only speaks up once a node is overloaded, but RFC 7068 also requires a way to share load levels when nothing is wrong, so that nodes can pick servers wisely and avoid overload in the first place.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes piggyback a grouped Load AVP on answer messages. It carries a type (HOST or PEER), a value from 0 to 65535 modelled on DNS SRV weights, and the identity of the sender.
tldr.outcome: Load reports are hints, not commands. Receivers use them for server selection, next-hop selection and load balancing, and how they do so is left to the implementation.

today: RFC 8583 is a Proposed Standard on the standards track and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7683 and uses the SourceID AVP from RFC 8581.

sections.title: The Gap Left by DOIC
sections.content:
RFC 7068 lists requirements for overload control in Diameter. The Diameter Overload Information Conveyance mechanism (DOIC, RFC 7683) meets most of them, but not Req 23 and Req 24.

Req 23 asks for enough information to let a load-balancing node divert rejected or throttled messages to the upstream nodes most likely to have spare capacity. Req 24 asks for a way to indicate load levels even when not in an overload condition, so that nodes can prevent overload from happening.

The DIME Working Group deliberately left these out of DOIC. A principal reason was that the group did not agree on a general approach for conveying load information, so it deferred the problem to an extension or a separate mechanism. This RFC is that mechanism.
sections.eli5: The first system only told you when a cashier was already swamped. This one lets cashiers say how busy they are at any time, so problems can be avoided.

sections.title: Load Versus Overload
sections.content:
The RFC starts by separating two ideas that people often mix up. A node always has a load, which can be effectively zero, effectively full, or anywhere between. Overload, by contrast, is an exceptional condition. The two can also disagree: a node may normally run at a fully loaded level without being overloaded, and another may declare itself overloaded without being fully loaded.

The second difference is what the report asks of the receiver. A DOIC Overload Report (OLR) is a kind of contract: the reacting node must reduce the offered load. Load information is only a hint. The receiver may use it for load balancing, as input to some overload abatement techniques, or to guess whether the sender will soon be overloaded. It may even decide to increase the offered load.

The RFC names two main uses. One is diversion, where traffic moved away from an overloaded node needs to be spread over candidates according to their load. The other is ordinary server selection and next-hop selection when no overload exists. A node will need to handle both load reports and overload reports from the same peer, and the overload report always obliges the reacting node to cut traffic.
sections.eli5: Being busy is normal for a cashier. Being swamped is an emergency. A busy sign is a hint, while a swamped sign is a request to send fewer people.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Load Report
sections.content:
As with DOIC, load information rides along on existing Diameter applications by attaching Load AVPs to messages. There are two main differences from DOIC. First, there is no capability negotiation. A sender just includes the information, and if no node supports the mechanism it is ignored. Second, DOIC reports travel end to end, while load reports come in two types.

  • A host-load report describes the endpoint that sent the answer. It travels end to end, so any node doing server selection can use it.
  • A peer-load report is used when choosing the next-hop node. It matters only to the adjacent peer and is removed by the first supporting node that receives it.

Because reports can pass through nodes that do not support the mechanism, every report includes the identity of the node it describes. A receiver can then check that a report really came from its peer.

The load value follows the DNS SRV weight style of RFC 2782, with a range of 0-65535. This lets Load values and SRV weights feed the same distribution algorithm. Note the direction: a higher value means a lower load. A node with zero load would send 65535, and a node that is 100% loaded would send 0. How the value is calculated, and how often reports are sent, are implementation decisions.
sections.eli5: Some notes say how busy one cashier is and are passed all the way to the shopper. Other notes only matter to the person standing next to the cashier and get thrown away after one stop. A big number means very free, and zero means completely full.

sections.title: Theory of Operation
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an example network where a client C reaches a server S[n] via agents A1 and A4. When S[n] answers, it includes a host-load report naming itself as the source. If A4 supports the mechanism and does server selection, it stores that load in its routing information. Either way it leaves the host-load report in the message. A4 then adds its own peer-load report and forwards the answer to A1.

A1 handles each report separately. For the peer-load report, it compares the source named in the report with the DiameterIdentity of the node the message arrived from. If they differ, the report is discarded; if they match, the load is saved. In both cases A1 strips the peer-load report. The host-load report is stored only if A1 does server selection, and is left in the message. A1 then inserts its own peer-load report and sends the answer to C, which repeats the same steps.

If a node in the path does not support the mechanism, it relays the Load AVPs unchanged.
sections.eli5: The server shouts how busy it is, and each helper along the way passes that note on while adding a small note about itself. Each helper reads only the note from the person right next to it.

sections.title: What Reporting and Reacting Nodes Must Do
sections.content:
A Diameter endpoint that supports the mechanism MUST include a load report of type HOST in enough answer messages that all consumers get timely updates. It MUST put its own DiameterIdentity in the SourceID AVP and its Load value in the Load-Value AVP. A Diameter agent MUST do the same with a report of type PEER. The Load value should reflect available load independently of server weight, so that a given value means the same spare capacity whichever node sent it.

A reacting node MUST be ready to handle messages with no reports, with only a peer report, with only a host report, or with both. A node that is not responsible for server selection SHOULD ignore HOST reports, and one that is responsible SHOULD save the Load value. For a PEER report, the node MUST check the SourceID against the identity of the connection the message came from, and MUST ignore the report if they do not match. A Diameter agent MUST strip all PEER reports it receives, so exactly one PEER report, from the sending node, is in any answer it sends.

How routing decisions use the information is up to the implementation, but the distribution algorithm MUST behave similarly to the weight handling in RFC 2782.

The RFC also covers growth. When a node is added, it starts by advertising its load and downstream nodes can ramp up traffic smoothly. When a node is removed in a controlled way, traffic can be reduced gradually, though simple load information would not be enough for that.
sections.eli5: Servers must announce their own busyness and helpers must announce theirs. Everyone must check who wrote a note before trusting it, and helpers must throw away the neighbour notes after reading them.

sections.title: The Load AVPs
sections.content:
The Load AVP (code 650) is of type Grouped and holds three optional pieces plus any extension AVPs. Load-Type (code 651) is Enumerated, with HOST as 0 and PEER as 1. Load-Value (code 652) is Unsigned64 and holds the relative load, in the range 0-65535, with a higher value meaning a lower load. SourceID identifies the Diameter node that sent the report and is defined in RFC 8581.

None of these AVPs sets the V flag. The M-bit usage for a given AVP in a given command may be defined by the application, as in the Diameter base protocol.

The mechanism can be extended. New AVPs for load reports SHOULD be defined as extensions to the Load AVP, and the grouped AVP extension rules of RFC 6733 apply.
sections.eli5: A load note is a small form with three boxes: what kind of note it is, a number saying how free you are, and who wrote it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Load information can be sensitive. An unauthorized recipient might infer the topology of a Diameter network, spot a heavily loaded node as a tempting target for denial-of-service attacks, or use the reports as feedback on how well an attack is going.

Because routing decisions depend on these values, erroneous or malicious reports can hurt the network, including Diameter agents that maliciously change Load values. Operators must be able to avoid sending load information to nodes not authorized to receive it. Diameter only authenticates nodes at the transport level and has no end-to-end security mechanism, so any solution that sends load information to non-peer nodes needs a transitive-trust model.
sections.eli5: Telling everybody how busy you are can help the wrong people, and a fake note could send shoppers to the wrong line. So you should only share the notes with those you trust.
